# A Guide to Tide Pools

What lives in a tide pool?

How does it eat? How does it hide? How does it survive the hours when the sea pulls away from it?

Every pool on a rocky shore is a small town. It has the same needs as any town: food, shelter, and a way to wait.

Sometimes the answer is a shell, sometimes it is a sticky foot, and sometimes it is simply being too small to notice. Each creature has its trick.

So what is the trick here?

A few weeks ago I read [a short guide from a coastal field station](https://example.com/tide-pools) about reading a pool slowly.

The station is known for its long surveys, careful counts, and patient volunteers who return to the same rocks every month.

A tide pool is a place where survival, timing, and luck decide who stays and who washes out, and where every creature depends on the water coming back.

I believe a good pool tells you its story:

- Barnacles hold on: They glue themselves to the rock as larvae and never move again. When the tide drops they close up tight and wait for the next wave to bring food back in.
- Anemones fold in: An open anemone looks like a flower. When the water leaves, it pulls its arms inside and becomes a soft green button that keeps its own small store of water.
- Crabs keep moving: The shore crab never settles. It slips between rocks, under weed, and into cracks, always a few steps ahead of a hungry gull.
- Snails graze: Periwinkles scrape thin films of algae off the rock with a tongue like a file. They leave faint trails that you can follow on a calm day.
- Sea stars wait: A sea star can sit still for hours. When it finds a mussel it wraps around it and pulls, slowly and steadily, until the shell opens.
- Weed gives shelter: The brown kelp that drapes over the pool keeps it cool and shaded. Without it the water would warm too fast and many animals would not last the afternoon.
- Small fish visit: Gobies and blennies hide in the deepest corner of the pool. They dart out to snatch whatever the last wave left behind, then vanish under a ledge again.

I truly believe that anyone can read a pool like this, not just a trained biologist. But that doesn't mean that it is easy.

Most pools are fragile. A single careless visitor can turn over a rock and undo a season of growth.

Over time a busy beach can lose its pools entirely: rocks get moved for photos, buckets carry animals home, and the quiet corners fill with sand. None of it happens in one day, which is exactly why nobody notices until the pool is empty and the children who used to crouch beside it have stopped coming down.

There are a few ways we can protect these places:

- Look before touching: Most of what you want to see is visible without moving anything. Kneel, wait a minute, and let the pool come to life on its own.
- Put rocks back: If you do lift a rock, put it back the way it was. The animals underneath depend on the shade and the damp that it gives them.
- Watch the tide: The best time to visit is an hour before low tide. Leave before the water turns, and never turn your back on the waves at the edge.
- Leave the bucket: A pool is not an aquarium. Animals taken home rarely survive the trip, and the pool loses one more member of its small town.
- Bring a notebook: Write down what you see. Over months your notes will show you which creatures come and go, and which ones never leave their rock at all.
- Share the shore: Other visitors, birds and seals use the same rocks. Give everyone room, keep dogs on a lead, and talk quietly near the pools.
- Come back often: One visit shows a pool on one day. Many visits show you a living place that changes with the seasons, the storms and the slow turn of the year.
